meta.ethics: The imaging unit is a theatrical inspection metaphor. It reads what a document shows and says. It does not detect skill, character, initiative or team compatibility, and nothing here is automated analysis: the notes were written for this exhibit from a reading of the supplied PDFs, and the scan is an animation that computes nothing.
meta.entranceNote: Three real student portfolio projects are on file. The unit separates what a portfolio shows from what it documents, and both from what no document can show.
meta.consent: I understand the unit examines documents, not people.

specimens.title: Bachat Basics
specimens.subtitle: Financial-literacy kit and workshop for underprivileged urban women · business plan pitch
specimens.recommended: Most documented process of the three: seven changes attributed to user testing (p. 13), pretotypes and prototypes (pp. 10–12) and a named version two (p. 16).
specimens.fileNote: The file name names one team member and the PDF’s author field shows another member’s design-tool account. Neither says who made which part.
specimens.spelling: The project name appears as both “Bachat” and “Bacchat” in the file.

folder.visible: Kit, guidebook, card game, app wireframes

visible.t: A physical kit, photographed: sari-box packaging, picture-led guidebook, scenario card game, piggy bank and helpline card.
A bilingual identity: Devanagari and Latin letter blocks.
Whether the dummy ATM and kit-packaging images are physical prototypes or digital renders. Looking can’t settle it, and the page doesn’t say.
visible.ask: Which of the prototypes on page 10 were physically built, and which are renders?

context.t: Problem framed as a financial-literacy gap for underprivileged urban women, with eight root-cause areas mapped.
Existing programmes reviewed and their gaps named (low-literacy formats, discreet learning, fear of mistakes).
Primary users, research findings and unmet needs set side by side.
Sources for the headline statistics (79%, 32%, 31%). None are cited in the file.
context.ask: Where do the statistics on page 2 come from?

evidence.t: Research findings summarised: fear of mistakes at ATMs and with UPI, bank accounts left unused, confidence growing through guided, hands-on practice.
User testing reported, with seven outcomes and photographs of four participants with the kit.
How the research and testing were done: method, number of participants, where and when, and the raw notes.
evidence.ask: How many people tested the kit, where, and how were their reactions recorded?

evidence.t: Who on the team planned and ran the testing.
evidence.ask: Who ran the user testing, and what did each person observe?

choices.t: The sari box: privacy at home chosen over a visible “learning kit”.
The app demoted to an optional parallel channel because it required confidence the kit didn’t.
The piggy bank repositioned as a short-term habit starter rather than long-term storage.
Costed at ₹89,300 for 100 kits, one dummy ATM and four workshops; risks listed with mitigations.
Directions that were considered and rejected before the ones on page 13.
choices.ask: What did you try that didn’t make it into the kit?

change.t: Pretotypes (paper piggy bank, pocket saving calendar, packaging, dummy ATM) followed by printed prototypes (guidebook, card game, sari-box kit).
Seven changes attributed to user testing, each tied to a part of the business model.
A “version two” sari-box kit named as the minimum viable product, and finalising version 2 placed first on the roadmap.
Dates, the order of the changes, and version one shown beside version two.
change.ask: What did version one of the kit look like, and when did it change?

people.t: Five team members credited on the cover: Anagha Shetty, Avishi Maru, Kavya Nair, Nikita Chandramouli, Nishita Bajaj.
Who did what: individual roles and contributions.
people.ask: Which parts of the kit, research and plan did each person lead?

people.t: How the team divided work, disagreed and decided.
people.ask: Tell me about a decision the team disagreed on. How was it settled?

beyond.t: Results from a pilot. The impact metrics and launch plan are targets and plans, not measured outcomes.
beyond.ask: Has any part of the kit been used outside testing? What happened?

beyond.t: Initiative, reliability, how each person takes feedback, what they would be like to work with. The unit examines documents, not people.
beyond.ask: What feedback changed your mind on this project, and how did you respond?

hotspots.title: The kit, photographed
hotspots.note: A physical, assembled kit: box, guidebook, cards and piggy bank.

hotspots.title: Why a sari box
hotspots.note: Designed to blend into the home and protect privacy, so learning can continue without household scrutiny.

hotspots.title: App wireframes
hotspots.note: Five low-fidelity screens. Page 13 later reframes the app as optional.

hotspots.title: Paper pretotype: piggy bank
hotspots.note: A rough paper box, photographed. Compare the finished piggy bank on page 12.

hotspots.title: Pretotype: pocket saving calendar
hotspots.note: A hand-made paper calendar with pockets. It does not appear among the prototypes on page 12.

hotspots.title: Built or rendered?
hotspots.note: The dummy ATM image could be a physical model or a render. The page doesn’t say, and looking can’t settle it.

hotspots.title: Packaging: mock-up?
hotspots.note: This box image could be a digital mock-up. The final kit on page 12 is a sari box instead.

hotspots.title: Guidebook and card game
hotspots.note: Printed spreads in Hindi and illustrated scenario cards.

hotspots.title: The sari box
hotspots.note: The packaging that replaced the printed kit box: page 13 ties it to privacy concerns raised in testing.

hotspots.title: Scenario cards
hotspots.note: Icon-led cards with minimal reading, the form page 13 says testing pushed them towards.

hotspots.title: Helpline card
hotspots.note: Public helpline numbers listed on a pocket card.

hotspots.title: Change 1: guidebook
hotspots.note: Long text felt heavy, so the guidebook became shorter and picture-led.

hotspots.title: Change 2: card game
hotspots.note: Users understood icons faster, so the game was redesigned with minimal reading.

hotspots.title: Change 3: privacy
hotspots.note: Privacy concerns at home led to the sari box with a hidden compartment.

hotspots.title: Change 4: piggy bank
hotspots.note: Unsure about capacity, so it was repositioned as a short-term habit starter.

hotspots.title: Change 5: guided practice
hotspots.note: Users preferred guided practice, so in-person workshops became the main channel.

hotspots.title: Change 6: the app
hotspots.note: The kit fitted users’ routines but the app needed confidence, so it became optional.

hotspots.title: Change 7: validation
hotspots.note: Positive reactions to the ATM and sari box are reported. How many users, and how they were asked, isn’t.

hotspots.title: Participants (blurred here)
hotspots.note: Four photographs of participants with the kit. Blurred in this exhibit. The file gives no count, method, place or date for testing.

hotspots.title: Version two
hotspots.note: The “version two” sari-box kit, a working dummy ATM and the workshop curriculum form the MVP.

hotspots.title: Targets, not results
hotspots.note: Every figure here is a target. No pilot results are reported.

hotspots.title: Risks and mitigations
hotspots.note: Household conflict, digital hesitation, wear and tear, low attendance, each with a response.

hotspots.title: Costing
hotspots.note: ₹89,300 in total: 100 kits, one dummy ATM, four workshops, transport.

versions.note: Documented sequence: rough paper and mock-up pretotypes, then printed and assembled prototypes. Page 13 attributes seven of the changes to user testing. Dates are not given.

specimens.subtitle: A service-design story for Nature’s Basket

folder.context: Grocery store experience · customer, staff, manager
change: No drafts or iterations in the file

pagesText.t: Cover: the title as a film-poster parody, “a Nature’s Basket story”.
Cast of six characters: customer, store associate, manager, marketer, CEO and “the result”.
Problem: shopping feels disconnected, unguided and unrelated to people and community.
The associate’s product knowledge lives in his head, not in the system.
The manager sees sales and stock, but not how the store is experienced.
Reframe: three problems are one service.
Scenario: the customer must cook a Japanese dinner to impress a guest.
The trip starts before the store: inspiration, saved journeys, reminders (app screens).
Mission-based shopping with in-store navigation (app screens).
Themed in-store station for building a ramen bowl.
Kiosk design.
Shopping by intention: date night, hosting, high protein, comfort food.
Shelf labels that tell origin, taste and pairing.
The associate as a trusted guide rather than a salesperson.
A staff learning “passport” with badges and rewards.
A five-step guidance routine: ask, filter, recommend, explain, pair.
Food circles and monthly events to build community.
A physical Discovery Passport collecting experiences.
Remembering the customer between visits: event, remember, suggest, return.
The manager’s service walk: price, flow, staff, discovery, counter.
Fix ordinary friction before adding extraordinary moments.
A relationship dashboard for the CEO.
Proposed measures: discovery, confidence, experience, connection, return, value.
Closing pun on the title.

visible.t: Visible in the file (not reproduced here): app screens, an in-store station, kiosk, shelf labels, staff and customer passports, a manager dashboard.

context.t: The problem is framed as one service seen from three sides: customer, associate and manager.

choices.t: Operations before delight: fix missing prices, blocked aisles and unattended counters first.
Proposed measures for whether the service is working.
